title: Duchy of Naples
capsule: The Duchy of Naples emerged in 661 as a Byzantine administrative territory on the Campanian coast that Lombard expansion had failed to overrun, governed by a duke (dux) appointed from Constantinople, with Basil as its first recorded holder. Duke Stephen II broke with Constantinople in 763, placing Naples under papal suzerainty; under Sergius I (r. c. 840–864) the succession became hereditary, rendering Naples de facto independent. The duchy demonstrated sustained military capacity, contributing to the defeat of an Arab fleet at the Battle of the Garigliano in 915 with its allies. Sergius VII surrendered to Roger II of Sicily in 1137, incorporating Naples into the Norman kingdom after over four centuries of autonomous rule.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core urban territory is well attested through Byzantine and papal documents; the duchy's rural hinterland boundaries fluctuated with Lombard pressure and are incompletely mapped in scholarship.
